title: Master Class | Alekhine (The Better Scandi) | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We try another Alekhine — a knight to f6, hoping White commits with e5 rather than a quiet knight to c3.
White plays e5.
And the idea: a knight to d5 — the ultimate hypermodern opening, where you refuse to touch your center for a few moves and try to get White to overextend.
White plays a bishop to c4 — a move, but not the best; we'll cover the theory later.
A knight to b6 — where this knight belongs in the Alekhine — attacking the bishop, so it retreats and loses a tempo.
A bishop to e2 is passive. Our strategy doesn't change: White's e5 pawn is a hook we'll use to contest the center while developing.
The most accurate move is d6, saying we want to remove that e5 pawn — and if we do, White has no central control left.
White plays d4 to fight for the center. Now a knight to c6 makes sense — the way to stop your pieces being trampled by pawns is to combine piece moves with pawn moves, so the pawns act as anchors.
Is d5 a problem before we play the knight to c6? Look carefully — no, because d5 loses control of e5 and drops a pawn.
White plays a knight to f3. Now we transform the position — a bishop to g4 is obvious, but in the spirit of positional chess we take on e5 into an endgame.
We capture on e5.
If White recaptures with the knight, a knight to d4 wins a pawn; he takes with the pawn instead.

We trade queens, and now that e5 pawn becomes a huge weakness — that's the whole point of the Alekhine: White has more central control, but he'll likely lose that pawn or wreck his pieces defending it.
How do we pressure e5? First its defender, the knight — a bishop to g4.
Not e6, which would be passive and lock the bishop in — we'll play e6 later.

Critical moment: don't just grab on f3 and e5, because it drops the b7 pawn — and even if it didn't, giving up that g4 bishop isn't clearly worth a pawn. The threat is stronger than the execution: keeping him tortured by the weak pawn beats winning it and relieving him.
So we castle long, defending b7, keeping pressure on the bishop and mobilizing our knight. Now we threaten to take on f3, but we could also just keep pressing with e6.
White plays a knight to d2 — a bit of a panic; a knight to g5 would have dropped the bishop to two attackers.
We win a piece — take the bishop, which also pins the rook, rather than traveling to g4.
We take the pawn on e5 — otherwise a knight to a3 could defend.
White plays a knight to c3. Now we just play e6.
e6, to get our bishop out.
White plays a knight to e4, untangling. We could take the rook, but I like just developing — trading on your own terms forces the opponent into uncomfortable decisions.
A bishop to e7 is fine — its main job here is to connect the rooks; it restricts the e4 knight and controls g5. Not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
White plays a bishop to f4, also controlling d8, and attacks our knight — we can move it with tempo.
A knight to g6, in Alekhine spirit — and it sets a trap: a bishop to g3 loses a piece.
White sees it and plays a bishop to e3 — little relief. That e4 knight has been a recurring theme: a central piece still vulnerable to pawns.
So f5, attacking the e4 knight — it has no good squares; the ones near it touch our e7 bishop, and its only defender is the bishop, a vulnerable undefended piece we can dislodge from e3.
White found a creative solution — a knight to c5, attacking c6, so if f4 he has a knight capture on e6 counterattacking our rook. We have to calculate.
Two pieces for a rook with no other rook pair usually favors the rook, but here the minors are super active, so we go for it — also to show how to play with this common imbalance.
White captures on e6 — he's playing very well.
We recapture on e3.
The king recaptures on f2. Now, to be surgical...
...a bishop check on c5, improving the bishop first — an intermediate move.
You're always hunting for intermediate moves, which can be tactical or positional — like improving the bishop before taking the knight.
A rook check on d1.
The king goes to e7 — the only good square.
White made a small error bringing his king backward — you shouldn't do that in the endgame — and he trades the knights.
We recapture on d5.
We recapture with the rook, reaching bishop and knight against rook with equal pawns — a great imbalance.
White attacks the bishop; we drop it back to d6 to attack the pawn. In these situations piece activity decides everything.
White plays c4.
A bishop capture on h2 nets a free pawn — and if he relies on a rook to h5, we have a sexy idea.
A rook to h5 forks the bishop and pawn — and how do we punish it?
A rook in the corner looks invincible, but it isn't — a bishop to f4 threatens to trap it. Rooks can be caught by minor pieces.
White grabs on h7.

A bishop to h6 — the rook is trapped: the knight covers its escape, the bishop covers the h-file, and our king will walk to g8 to finish it. He can try to ram the pawn, but there's no time — that's jail.
Don't free the rook by moving carelessly — the king walk is a brutal idea.
It's over — he has to take the bishop.
Now we're up a full knight.
A knight check on e5 to win the pawn.
Bring the knight back, and there are many ways to win.
We bring the king up, he gives us access to the pawn, and we push — had he defended, I'd just create a passer and distract his king. He resigns.
A great game. The bishop to c4 is sub-optimal for White.
The main line is d4.
Then Black plays d6 and White plays c4.
And you get this kind of position.
Black recaptures with either pawn — the c-pawn recapture is more adventurous, something to cover later.
The Alekhine is a great weapon in the 1600-1700 range if you want to spice up your repertoire, both positional and tactical. In our game a bishop to b2 was passive — b3 was better.

Then d6 — don't overthink it; it just removes e5, grabs some center, and opens the bishop, a normal developing move. After d4 and a knight to c6, don't slip into passivity with an early e6, or White tramples the center and you're miserable — that's the downside of the Alekhine if you don't play it well.
People either love the Alekhine or try it and hate it — the trick is not to treat d6 as some special move.
It just controls some center and opens the bishop — a typical developing move played in all openings.
So d6, d4, a knight to c6, a knight to f3...
...and we take on e5, trading queens.
White should have recaptured on d6 and played c4, resembling the main line — a tempo up for us, and then we fianchetto.
After the queen trade and a bishop to g4, White should have played a bishop to f4.
Either there or earlier — the knight to d2 was far too passive.
After a bishop to f4...
...we'd play e6, get the bishop out, maybe bring a knight to d5 — White is uncomfortable because e5 is a permanent weakness, sticking out like a sore thumb, and Black is slightly better.
So here he gives us the pawn...
...e6, a knight to e4, a bishop to e7 covering the squares.
A bishop to f4, a knight to g6 — and there was one little issue.
A knight to c4 might support a knight to b5, and I was looking at those lines.
This is actually checkmate — we'd have played c6, but it felt a bit unpleasant.
So instead we went a knight to g6, actively retrieving the bishop.
Had he gone a bishop to g3, as I hinted...
...then f5, and the bishop is trapped.
That's completely winning, so he goes a bishop to e3.
And we go f5, dislodging the knight from e4.
After the rook trade and a knight to c5, why is playing a knight to c5 immediately less accurate? Think about it.
The problem: if we play f4 it transposes to the game...
...but its power comes from the knight attacking the rook — otherwise it's just a pawn and we take the bishop. We'd capture on d1 and play f4.

Why give up the open file? Tactics trump general considerations — a bishop to d4, e5, and the bishop is trapped; if it moves back we take the knight, and if a knight capture on c6, we take the bishop.
So it was a good decision to take the rook first with a knight to c5.

And that forces us to win it out. He went backward with the king, which is fine, but I probably should have gone forward. When he traded the knights he collapsed — that c3 knight should have gone to e4, which is exactly why the bishop on c5 is a sitting duck.
